aliases: Posterior Basement Membrane of the Corneal Endothelium

content.definition: Descemet's membrane is the thick, homogeneous basal lamina secreted by the corneal endothelium, forming the smooth posterior boundary of the corneal stroma. It appears around the second month of gestation and grows throughout life — from about 3-4 μm at birth to about 5 μm in childhood and 10-12 μm in the adult — and it is composed of type IV collagen rather than the type I collagen of the stroma.
content.location: It lies between the posterior stroma and the corneal endothelium, to whose cells it is attached by modified hemidesmosomes and desmosomes. Peripherally it ends at Schwalbe's line, which marks the anterior limit of the drainage angle; there it is continuous with the trabecular meshwork lining. A prominently placed Schwalbe's line (posterior embryotoxon) is visible in about 15-20% of individuals.
layers: Anterior third (fetal banded zone): laid down in utero, with a banded ultrastructure of 100-110 nm periodicity — compared with the 64 nm periodicity of stromal type I collagen — and triangular projections; banding is evident from about the fifth month of gestation, when the zone is about 3.1 μm thick
Posterior two-thirds (postnatal zone): added after birth by the endothelium as a homogeneous, unbanded layer responsible for the progressive age-related thickening
content.blood_supply: Avascular — like all layers of the cornea, Descemet's membrane contains no blood vessels; the nearest vessels belong to the pericorneal/limbal vascular plexus at the corneoscleral junction.
content.venous_drainage: None — the membrane is avascular; venous return is peripheral, via the anterior ciliary veins at the limbus.
content.histology_summary: Descemet's membrane is the endothelium's own basal lamina and behaves like one: it thickens throughout life by continuous endothelial secretion, from about 3-4 μm at birth through about 5 μm in childhood to 10-12 μm in the adult (Tripathi; Wulle), and it is composed of type IV collagen. Ultrastructurally it has two strata: an anterior third — the fetal banded layer with 100-110 nm banding and triangular projections, banding being apparent from about the fifth month of gestation when the zone is about 3.1 μm thick — and a posterior two-thirds of homogeneous postnatal material. By the third month of development a lamina lucida (about 37.5 nm) and a lamina densa (about 36.7 nm) can be distinguished beneath the endothelium (Murphy, Alvarado & Juster). The endothelium is attached to it by modified hemidesmosomes and desmosomes; and — in marked contrast to Bowman's layer — after an interruption such as acute hydrops in keratoconus the membrane is repaired by the endothelium laying down a new basal lamina of matching type. Development (Wolff 17.2): further differentiation and growth of the membrane are accomplished by the sequential secretion of a series of individual 'membrane-units' that build up its multilayered structure (Fig 17.12). The process is rapid: although only one such layer is discernible at 12 weeks of gestation, approximately 10 layers are present by the sixth month and 30-40 layers at birth; short thin linear filaments (about 170 nm long and 40 nm in diameter) are laid down perpendicular to and between adjacent layers and are thought to function as cross-linking bridges that bind and pull the adjacent membrane-unit layers together, compacting this region of the membrane during the last trimester of gestation (Murphy, Alvarado and Juster, 1984). In flat sections the fibrils of the banded zone are arranged hexagonally and are interconnected with nodes and internodes of electron-dense material, producing a lamellar pattern of equilateral triangles with sides of about 110 nm; this unique organization identifies the anterior third of the membrane as the 'fetal' banded zone, which attains a maximum thickness of about 3 um at birth. Postnatally, a homogeneous fibrillogranular material - the posterior non-banded zone - constitutes the membrane and continues to thicken with age (Tripathi and Tripathi, 1984).
content.clinical_importance: Two classes of endothelial excrescences mark its posterior surface: peripherally, Hassall-Henle warts are a physiological age change, whereas central cornea guttata are abnormal and are associated with increased endothelial permeability and corneal oedema (Lorenzetti & Kaufman). The membrane can be ruptured — by birth trauma, by stretching in infantile glaucoma, or in acute hydrops of keratoconus — after which its rolled edges are repaired by endothelial regeneration of a new basal lamina. A prominent Schwalbe's line (posterior embryotoxon) marks its peripheral termination in about 15-20% of the population. Modern endothelial keratoplasty is built around this membrane: in DSAEK the donor tissue carries posterior stroma with Descemet's membrane and endothelium, while in DMEK only Descemet's membrane and the endothelium are transplanted.
